cells.tense: You are here, with a rough frame half-raised and the pen still in your hand.
cells.act: show someone the way you found
cells.ask: With the person you're helping build something, walk them through the route you took, then stop at the showing. Tell it once, plainly, and stop there.
cells.core: Something new is taking shape in your care, and you're good at the part that can't be faked: putting one piece on another until it stands. Around anything growing, that instinct shows up as scaffolding — a first rough frame a young thing can lean on while it decides what it is. Not a finished house. Enough to grow against.\n\nThat's the balance: you raise the frame and then you step back. The habit that holds it is showing someone the route you took and stopping at the showing — not walking it for them. Tell it once, plainly, and leave the next step theirs. What that gives the growing thing is a direction it can hold. The trick is that it stays theirs to walk.
cells.sheetLine: You raise the frame and the growing thing leans on it.
cells.verb: raising the frame around what is growing
cells.place: where you keep something growing that hasn't found its shape yet

cells.tense: By the time it is finished you already know how it will have to hold.
cells.act: leave the hollow ritual for the living one
cells.ask: Pick a step you keep in the care of something growing only out of habit — drop just that one — and then stay with what the dropping frees.
cells.core: The building runs past the thing that's growing. Around anything developing, you're adding the next beam before the last one has set — planning the pace, the next stage, the form it becomes, while it hasn't yet grown into the ground beneath it. It reads as care. From where the young thing stands, nothing gets to decide its own form.\n\nWhat loosens it is leaving one dead step behind. Pick a piece of the routine you keep going only because it's habit, and drop that single step. Then stay with what the space does. Don't fill it and don't replace it. The person growing something beside you may notice the gap before you do, and that's fine — what you're after is what the dropping frees.
cells.sheetLine: You build the roof before the walls have set.

cells.tense: The frame you started is still standing back there where you left it.
cells.act: decide it and act the same day, without explaining
cells.ask: Whatever the growing thing needs next — water, a shelf, a yes — settle it and do it the same day, and explain nothing to anyone.
cells.core: Around what's growing, no frame is going up. Things are kept going, kept safe, kept as they were — and the building that needs a first rough shape sits unfinished behind you. The knack for making structure out of something raw is in you. Here, it's standing down.\n\nNursing the gap won't bring it back. A decision moved will. Take whatever the growing thing actually needs and do it the same day you settle it, without telling anyone why. Then let it be done — no review, no justifying the call. That's not the finished frame; it's the first beam, and the first beam is what gets the rest moving. Something that stands gets built from a decision, not from a mood.
cells.sheetLine: You keep it safe, and nothing that grows gets a floor.

cells.tense: You are already building it, and by your own account it happened on its own.
cells.act: defend the direction you chose against the next push
cells.ask: Next time someone leans on the shape you're giving what you tend, hold it once — say what you decided and keep going.
cells.core: There is a frame going up around something you tend, and it is standing. The load-bearing calls were yours — the pacing, the order, the small refusals — and asked about it, you'd file that under keeping things from collapsing. The building is real. The name on it is missing.\n\nTo claim it, defend the direction you already chose. Next time someone leans on the shape you're giving this, hold it once — say what you decided, keep going, and meet the pressure as a settled thing. You don't have to prove it was yours. The frame holds whether or not you claim it, and holding your ground is how the claim gets made. What gets built stays yours either way.
cells.sheetLine: The frame holds, and the name on it is missing.
